In Ismaili spiritual teaching, the herald of this primordial prophecy is the First Intelligence, or Archangel ('Aql awwal), belonging to the heavenly fullness of beings, the Pleroma. Twelver Shiite spiritual teaching gives this being many titles: the Supreme Successor, the Pole of Poles, the Sublime Spirit (Ruh a'zam), the Supreme Pen, the Greatest Human (Insan kabir), and the True Adam (Adam haqiqi). These names tell us that the Heavenly Human of ancient spiritual traditions has become the Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat mohammadiya): the Muhammadan Word, the eternal model of the Prophet, the reality of Muhammad beyond time.

The earthly Prophet is not this eternal reality made flesh. Rather, he reveals it, as a mirror reveals an image. This is how Muhammad, as the Seal of the Prophets, manifests prophecy in its absolute and universal form. It is also the meaning of sayings endlessly repeated by Muslim spiritual thinkers: “The first thing God created was the Intelligence”; or “the Pen”; or “the Spirit.” All these forms come together in the saying: “The first thing God created was my Light”—the Muhammadan Light (Nur mohammadi).

And because this Heavenly Human, this True Adam, is the being God created in His own image ('ala surati-hi), the one who reflects that divine image can say: “Whoever has seen me has seen God.” This saying, with its clear echo of the Gospel, is also frequently attributed to the Imam. That is because the eternal reality of prophecy is, in fact, a unity made up of two inseparable sides.

We find this idea well before Ibn Arabi in the great works of Ismaili Shiite spiritual thought. There it appears as a pair: the First Intelligence and the Soul, or the first two Intelligences of the heavenly realm. The eternal prophetic reality (Haqiqat mohammadiya) has two faces, two dimensions. Its outward face is prophecy (nobowwat); its inner face is walayat, or the Imamate. This is why walayat is called “the inner dimension of prophecy” (see Chapter V above, on the Twelve Imams as the successive places where the prophetic mission is fulfilled). The same eternal reality is thus the source of both primordial prophecy and primordial walayat (asliya).

For that reason it is called the Spring of Life ('ayn al-Hayat). We must search for it through the darkness of nature and beyond the limits of religion understood only in its literal sense. What we seek is the spiritual Light that, as we have seen, was present in the Prophet's heart before his revelation took the form of words. That Light passes from his heart to the hearts of his spiritual heirs, the Twelve Imams.

As one text puts it: “The Spring of Life is the inner reality of the divine Name the Living (batin al-ism al-Hayy). Whoever truly understands it drinks from the Spring of Life; and whoever drinks that water will never die, because that person lives with divine life. Every living being in the world lives through the life of this Perfect Human (kamil, teleios), because his life is the very life of God.”

Like prophecy, walayat must therefore have both a universal, absolute aspect and a particular one. Its particular form had already appeared in all the Friends of God (Awliya) of earlier prophetic periods, when they were simply called prophets (Nabis). Its universal form, the inner reality of the Heavenly Human, appeared on Earth in the person closest to Muhammad by both spiritual and family ties: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the First Imam, the Commander of the Faithful.

And because the Twelve Imams share one spiritual essence (haqiqat), the Muhammadan Imamate as a whole is the Seal of walayat: the completion of the inner knowledge found within every prophetic religion. Just as Muhammad was the Seal of the Prophets, the Muhammadan Imamate seals walayat in two ways: through the First Imam, as the Seal of universal walayat, and through the Twelfth Imam, as the Seal of specifically Muhammadan walayat, or spiritual knowledge. This is why the First Imam could echo the Prophet's words and say: “I was already a wali”—a friend of God, an Imam who knows the inner truth of eternal prophecy—“when Adam was still between water and clay.”

These broad outlines help us understand a group of traditional sayings that insist on the unbreakable unity of Prophet and Imam, prophecy and spiritual initiation, outward meaning (zahir) and inner meaning (batin). In one saying, the Prophet declares: “Ali and I are one and the same Light.” In another: “Ali and I were one Light before God, fourteen thousand years before He created Adam.” These are not years measured by our calendars, of course, but the time of the heavenly world—the “absolutely subtle” time described by Qazi Sa'id Qommi.

Another saying explains the eternal Imam's relationship to the temporary mission of prophets who bring a law: “Ali was sent secretly alongside every prophet; with me, he was sent openly.” In other words, every prophetic religion has had an inner spiritual teaching, but its existence was kept hidden. The final Prophet's mission was different: he openly announced that this inner teaching existed, while leaving its instruction to the Imam. In a sermon of remarkable importance, the Khutbat al-Bayan, quoted earlier, the Imam declares: “I am the one who holds the secret of God's Messenger.” The Muhammadan Imamate is therefore the inner dimension of every earlier religion.

But this spiritual knowledge will only be fully revealed, without concealment or veil, at the return of the Mahdi, the Twelfth and final Imam. As the Seal of Muhammadan walayat, he also completes universal walayat.

These texts show us how the Shiite understanding of the Imams grows naturally out of its understanding of prophecy. They also reveal how closely the major themes of Shiite thought fit together. The idea of the Heavenly Human—the eternal reality of prophecy—helps us understand why the Imamate, through its knowledge of inner meanings, inherits prophecy. It also explains why the Imam's kind of knowledge is understood as a spiritual inheritance, unlike knowledge gathered from outside. This distinction is crucial.

Shiite spirituality reaches its height in personally discovering the truth of the saying: “Whoever knows himself”—his own soul—“knows his Lord,” which here means his Imam. Its goal is to discover one's own spiritual Guide, the one we must come to know if we are not to die having lived in unawareness. This is not knowledge we acquire from outside. It is something given to the soul as an inheritance.

To grasp the full meaning of knowledge inherited by the soul, we first need to understand how Shiite writers describe the passing of the Prophet's spiritual inheritance to the Imam. Above all, this means the passing of the Light that made the Prophet and the Imam a single, two-sided reality before either appeared on Earth. From the creation of Adam onwards, that Light—their shared Spirit (Ruh mohammadi)—was passed down through successive generations, kept free from every impurity, especially shirk, the ignorance that breaks apart the understanding of God's oneness. It reached Abd al-Muttalib, the common ancestor of Muhammad and Ali. In these two descendants, the original unity of Prophet and Imam finally appeared as two distinct people.

This helps explain why Shiite thinkers have had to repeat a point so often misunderstood, sometimes completely. No one was ever worthy of being an Imam or the Prophet's successor merely because he was related to the Prophet by blood (nisbat jismaniya, hissiya, suriya). Spiritual kinship (nisbat ma'nawiya) is also essential. And that kinship has its origin in the primordial Muhammadan Reality, which existed before the world. We have stressed this already.

What we have just read suggests that the Imams did not become Imams because they belonged to the Prophet's family. Rather, they had to belong to the Holy Family (ahl al-bayt) because they were already Imams. Their earthly family relationship simply makes visible a unity that existed among them in the heavenly world. It is never merely a matter of blood. From the beginning, it is a spiritual relationship.

This double kinship, both earthly and spiritual, together with each Imam's personal designation (nass) and freedom from error and sin (ismat), identifies the Twelve Imams as the Prophet's heirs (Awsiya). But they do not inherit his outward office of bringing a divine law. What they inherit is the inner reality of his mission.

We must always remember the definition: walayat is the inner dimension of prophecy. The inheritance consists of their knowledge and, just as importantly, the way in which they know. Their right to this inheritance goes back beyond their family relationship on Earth, to their existence in the heavenly realm before the world began. What passes to the Imams is not tanzil, the act of “bringing down” revelation, but ta'wil, the act of leading the words of revelation back to their source, so that their deeper meaning can be understood.

The Prophet's relationship with the First Imam—and, through him, with the other eleven—is expressed in an especially important saying. After the Battle of Khaybar, the Prophet is reported to have addressed Ali in these words:

If I were not afraid that some of my community might say about you what Christians say about Christ (Masih), I would tell people something about you today that would make them gather the dust from your footsteps wherever you went, hoping to find a remedy in it because of your extraordinary purity.

But let it be enough for you that you are part of me, just as I am part of you. Whoever inherits from you will therefore inherit from me. For you stand in relation to me as Aaron stood in relation to Moses, with this one difference: after me there will be no other prophet.

This saying confirms what we have been discussing. The eternal, essential reality (haqiqat) of the Seal of the Messengers and that of the Seal of God's Friends (Awliya), the bearers of spiritual knowledge, are one and the same. We see its outward prophetic dimension in the Prophet, and its inner dimension of walayat in the Twelve Imams. With that heavenly kinship established, let us look at how it is understood to appear in the visible world ('alam al-zahir).
Another saying, attributed to the Prophet, describes the Imam in these terms:
His secret is that he lives my life and dies my death. He is like a branch that my God planted with His own hand. God said to it, “Be,” and it was.

This image means that the Imam’s ancestry reaches upwards to the divine will; it is not simply the result of human birth. Earthly descent follows from that higher origin (2:111 and elsewhere). The saying continues:

So may God watch over Ali after I am gone, and over the heirs (Awsiya) who descend from me—the other eleven Imams. They will be the Guides (hodat), the Faithful, those accepted by God. God will give them my understanding and my knowledge. This means that they share my spiritual rank and are worthy to succeed me and to hold the Imamate.

What qualifies the Imams as the Prophet's heirs, then, is that they possess the same level of understanding and knowledge as he does. This is also why, as we have seen, each is called Qayyim al-Qur'an, the one who safeguards the Qur'an and keeps its meaning alive. For the mission of bringing divine law has ended. We said a moment ago that the Imams do not inherit that part of the Prophet's work. They inherit his walayat.

But this means that there must be something in the Prophet beyond his mission as the bearer of the law—something that Islam understood only in terms of outward rules cannot explain, but that Shiite spiritual teaching affirms. A very simple diagram makes this clear.

During his life on Earth, a Prophet who is also a Messenger (Nabi-Rasul) does not begin by holding the rank of Messenger. Abraham and Muhammad himself are the favourite examples. Such a person is first a wali, a Friend of God, or an 'arif, someone with direct spiritual knowledge. The two terms often appear together; we have called this kind of person a “gnostic.” He then becomes a Nabi, a prophet, and finally a Nabi-Rasul, a prophet who is also a Messenger. In Muhammad's case, this final stage is marked by the Angel's visible appearance. Being a Messenger (rasul) therefore requires both walayat and prophecy (nobowwat).
But someone can be a wali or a Nabi without ever becoming a Messenger who brings a divine law.

Shiite thinkers have reflected deeply on the relationship between these three spiritual states: walayat, the condition of being God's friend and receiving divine love; ordinary prophecy (nobowwat); and the Messenger's mission to establish a law (risalat). Moving from walayat to the mission of a lawgiving prophet means moving from the deepest inward level towards the outer world. Writers such as Haydar Amoli therefore picture the three states as circles within circles.

Walayat, the state of divine friendship, spiritual initiation, and inner knowledge, is the inner reality of prophecy. Prophecy, in turn, is the inner reality of the Messenger's lawgiving mission. And because closeness to God increases as spiritual life becomes more inward and less dependent on outward things, walayat has the highest rank of all. Haydar Amoli compares the outward mission of bringing a law (risalat) to the shell of a nut, inner prophecy (nobowwat batiniya) to its kernel, and walayat to the oil contained inside that kernel (see the diagram below).

A whole series of other comparisons expresses the same relationship. Moving from outside to inside, the three levels correspond to sharia, the outward observance of religious law; tariqat, the spiritual path; and haqiqat, the inner reality that is personally experienced. They also correspond to outward meaning, inner meaning, and the inner meaning within that inner meaning (batin al-batin). And they correspond to three levels of certainty: knowledge based on information ('ilm al-yaqin), certainty gained from seeing something for oneself ('ayn al-yaqin), and certainty gained through direct inner experience (haqq al-yaqin).

Before the Prophet could become a Messenger who brought a divine law (rasul), he therefore had to pass through the state of wali or 'arif. His walayat, the spiritual knowledge of one close to God, comes before his mission as a Messenger because it lies deeper within him. This is a principle our writers repeat constantly: walayat is higher than the state of a prophet who is also a Messenger, because it comes first and is the source of that mission.

Twelver Shiism, however, makes this comparison within the person of the Prophet himself. All three states are present in Muhammad, and he passes on to the Imams the walayat that forms his own deepest spiritual life. It is in the Prophet himself that walayat is higher than nobowwat.

Here, Haydar Amoli explains, lies an essential difference between Twelver Shiism and Ismaili Shiism—or at least the reformed Ismailism of Alamut, which proclaimed the Great Resurrection on 8 August 1164. Ismaili spiritual teaching takes the superiority of walayat over lawgiving prophecy to mean that the Imam himself is higher than the Prophet. Something of this tendency may have existed in Shiism from its beginnings; perhaps the Ismailis of Alamut were simply faithful to that older impulse.

But the result was a radical transformation of Islam into a religion of the Spirit alone. With the abolition of the sharia, divine law, it was almost an early arrival of the end of time: an anticipation of the liberation that the last Imam, the Mahdi, is to bring when he establishes the reign of the pure spiritual meaning of prophetic revelations.

Our concern here, however, is the middle path represented by Twelver Shiite spiritual thought. Although it continues to give the Prophet precedence over the Imam, there is always at least an underlying tendency to see the two as equals. The reason is that walayat stands above the lawgiving mission within the Prophet himself, and it is precisely this walayat that the Imam inherits. Prophet and Imam share one eternal essence in the heavenly world. The Prophet makes its outward side visible; the Imam, as the Seal of universal walayat, reveals its inner meaning.

We may recall the saying: “Ali was sent secretly alongside every prophet; with me, he was sent openly.” The Imam thus possesses, as his defining quality, the spiritual state that is higher than the Prophet's lawgiving mission within the Prophet himself. There is, of course, an ongoing tension in Shiism between spiritual knowledge and religious law. A prophetic religion remains truly prophetic only by continually reaching beyond the revealed words, while never cutting itself off from them.

We saw earlier that the Qur'an's spiritual reality (haqiqat) descended into the Prophet's heart before it took the form of words and letters—that is, before the Angel visibly appeared to “dictate” the text. Reflecting on this has led our thinkers into the deepest questions about how a prophet knows and experiences revelation. They find evidence that the Prophet remains inwardly a wali, whose spiritual state is higher than his mission as a lawgiving Messenger, in a famous saying cherished in both Shiism and Sufism:
There are moments when I am with God in such a way that neither a prophet who is a Messenger nor an Angel of the highest rank could contain what I experience.

Here the Prophet is no longer speaking as the Messenger who must receive the text that the Angel “brings down” (tanzil) and communicates to him (wahy). He is speaking as a wali, someone who knows God through direct, overwhelming experience. Haydar Amoli explains that the Prophet's inner being (batin al-nabi)—the part of him that belongs to his walayat—receives the divine outpouring (al-fayz min Allah) directly, without any intermediary. From there, it reaches his outward being, the level of prophecy.

At that second stage the Angel appears visibly while the Prophet is awake. At the first stage, before Gabriel—the Angel of Revelation who guides the Prophet—communicates anything outwardly, the Prophet encounters, at the deepest limit of his inner awareness, the “Gabriel of his own being.” That is what the claim means when it says that a wali draws from the very source from which the Angel receives the revelation he brings to the Messenger. The writers' account of prophetic experience thus reveals something essential for our theme: the guide who is also guided. To understand what the Angel means in prophetic knowledge, we must understand knowing through the heart and through the heart's “spiritual senses.”

Yet the Prophet is not himself meant to show the world that deepest state of his spiritual life, the state of walayat. It lies above his mission as a lawgiving Messenger and makes that mission possible. His prophetic message (risalat) has its source there. The one whose task it is to make walayat visible in the earthly world is the Imam.

At the deepest level, the Imam is formed from the same Light, the Light that is the Spirit and essence of eternal prophecy, the Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat mohammadiya). It is true that Islamic spiritual teaching, through this idea of the eternal Prophet, partly echoes the Verus Propheta, the “True Prophet,” of Jewish-Christian traditions: a true prophetic presence passing from one prophet to the next until it comes to rest in Muhammad, who follows Jesus.
But there is something else we must add. For Shiite prophetic philosophy, this eternal prophecy can never be separated from the way its meaning is understood and interpreted.

Prophetic revelation has “descended” from the heavenly heights with which the Prophet's deepest awareness (sirr) is in contact, taking the outward form of written and spoken words. This is tanzil. To discover the spiritual meaning of a text that has come down in this way, we must lead it back to its origin. That is what ta'wil, spiritual interpretation, means both in the word's origin and in the idea itself. For this reason, each prophet in the prophetic line is accompanied by an Imam in a parallel line of spiritual guides, beginning with Seth, the son and Imam of Adam.

Ta'wil is the Imam's task, because walayat—the inner reality of prophecy—is what the Imam inherits. This eternal walayat, which existed before our earthly world and will outlast it, is the foundation of the Imam's work of spiritual initiation as Qayyim al-Qur'an, the guardian who keeps the Qur'an alive. He must preserve the Book from being reduced to its literal words alone, as it would be in an Islam concerned only with outward observance. He does this by keeping it connected to the Spirit that first inspired it in the Prophet's heart—the Spirit that is its true meaning.

All this lies at the heart of the Shiite idea of the Imam as the Prophet's heir. The inheritance is not founded merely on descent by blood. Or rather, as we have seen, the earthly kinship linking the Twelve Imams to the Prophet is a visible sign of a relationship that already existed before this world. Their union in the heavenly realm is the model and source of every spiritual bond.
4. The Knowledge Inherited from the Prophets

We can now understand why certain views held even by Sunni Sufis appear not just strange but deeply troubling to Shiite thinkers. In their eyes, Sufis inherited the very idea of prophetic spiritual inheritance from Shiism and the teaching of the Imams, yet sometimes changed or stripped it of its meaning without seeming to notice. Shiites agree when Sufis say that prophecy bringing divine law has ended while walayat continues forever.

But they strongly disagree when non-Shiite Sufis say that the people who succeed the Prophet in his outward mission are the scholars of religious law—the “four imams” who founded the four main Sunni schools of law—while the Sufis themselves carry on walayat. Such a division assumes that outward religion (zahir) can continue independently of its inner meaning (batin). For Shiite thinkers, that is to deny inner prophecy (nobowwat batiniya) and the whole Shiite understanding of Islam.

We could quote endlessly from traditions in which the holy Imams show that they understand themselves to be spiritual heirs. Let us take just one, from the Fourth Imam, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who died around 95 AH (714 CE):

When we look at a person, we can recognize whether faith or hypocrisy is really present in them. The names of our Shiites—our faithful followers—are written down alongside the names of their ancestors. God has received a pledge (mithaq) from us and from them (see Section III.2 above). They walk the path we walk. They enter by the gate through which we enter. We are the Nujaba, the noble spiritual leaders.

We are named in God's Book. Of all human beings, we are closest to God's Book and closest to God's religion. We are the ones for whom this religion was established. For God says in His Book: “He has established for you a religion—the one He formerly entrusted to Noah, the one We have revealed to you, O Muhammad, and the one We entrusted to Abraham (42:11), Ishmael, Isaac, and Jacob.” We, then, are the ones who know. Knowledge has been passed down to us because we have been made the keepers of their knowledge. We are the heirs of the prophets; we are the heirs of the ulu'l-'azm, the six great lawgiving prophets among God's Messengers.

This makes the meaning of the inheritance quite clear. What the prophets pass on to the Imams is prophetic knowledge itself. The Imams are therefore the goal towards which the institutions established by the prophets were directed, for the Imams know their inner meaning. And their Shiites, their followers, “walk the same path and enter through the same gate.” There could hardly be a clearer statement: any philosophy that grows out of Shiism will be a prophetic philosophy.

Whenever the Imams speak of “our Shiites” in these traditions, they do not mean people who are related to them by blood. Haydar Amoli is emphatic about this. It is not enough to be a Sayyid, a descendant of Ali or Fatima. Physical descent alone gives no claim to an inheritance that is spiritual rather than outward. Blood ties can fail, as they did for the son of Noah who was not saved from the Flood. “Noah, this son is not one of yours” (11:48). Without the inner kinship (monasabat) that comes from taking up the spiritual path (tariqat), a person lacks the very capacity to receive the inheritance.

This capacity can also belong to those known as Uwaysis: people who, without an earthly shaykh or a human spiritual master like themselves, have been guided inwardly by the Imam. Its outstanding example is Salman the Persian, Salman the Pure (Salman Pak). Born the son of a Zoroastrian knight, he became a Christian and went in search of the True Prophet. The Prophet—or, in another attribution, the First Imam—declared of him: “Salman belongs to us, the people of the House (Salman minna ahl al-Bayt).” Salman became “a member of the Prophet's Family” not through physical descent (nisbat suriya), but through spiritual kinship (nisbat ma'nawiya).

Yet one cannot become a spiritual member of a family defined only by blood. For this inclusion to make sense, that family must itself be understood as a spiritual family. Haydar Amoli therefore insists that Salman's adoption shows what “Family” or “House” (Bayt) really means here. It is not the outward, biological household (bayt suri), which includes wives and children. It is the “Family of knowledge, spiritual insight, and wisdom” (Bayt al-'ilm wa'l-ma'rifat wa'l-hikmat).

Of course, this assumes that such a family exists. Haydar Amoli answers that it does: it is the family of the holy Imams. He compares the Prophet to a father by blood and the Imam to a spiritual father (ab ma'nawi). Family descent has no importance in the next world. In the same way, the outward connection with the Prophet as Messenger—the obligation to follow the sharia—falls away in the next world.

What remains important is spiritual kinship, created by the bond with the Imam and therefore with the spiritual reality of prophetic revelation. The Imam is the source of the spiritual relationship that Salman represents. Imam Ja'far puts it strikingly when he speaks of his own lineage: “My walayat—my bond of spiritual devotion—to the Commander of the Faithful matters more than the blood relationship that makes me his descendant (walayati li-Amiri'l-mu'minin khayr min wiladati min-ho).” This single saying brings together everything we have established so far.

But the Sunni Sufi tradition offers teachings that a Shiite thinker such as Haydar Amoli finds shocking. Consider Dawud Qaysari, a commentator on Ibn Arabi who died in 751 AH (1350 CE). He divides the Prophet's heirs into two groups. The first belongs to outward religion (zahir) and the sharia: legal scholars, teachers of religious law, and specialists in its outward requirements (olama' al-zahir).

The second belongs to inner religion (batin) and walayat: the Friends of God (Awliya) in general. Haydar Amoli is astonished. Qaysari says nothing about the Imams held to be free from error, whose position as the bearers of both universal and particular walayat, and as the Prophet's heirs, is established—within Shiite tradition—by transmitted sayings, theology, and philosophy. How, he asks, could they simply be left out? Yet this omission has a long history, going back to the point when Sufism began speaking about walayat without naming the source from which the idea came.
That source has been so thoroughly passed over, Haydar Amoli argues, that “Friends of God” has come to mean all believers without distinction.

But faith in its fullest sense is impossible without walayat. And walayat itself would be unthinkable without the Imams, those “Friends of God” in whom divine love first takes a form that can be known (see Chapter VII below). It would also be unthinkable without the spiritual Family into which everyone who follows Salman's example is welcomed.

Qaysari goes further. Without hesitation, he identifies the Prophet's heirs with the people commonly called the “four imams” in Sunni Islam. Here imam no longer has its special Shiite meaning. It means the four founders of the major Sunni schools of law: Abu Hanifa, founder of the Hanafi school (see the note on his moving encounter with Imam Ja'far); Ahmad ibn Hanbal, founder of the Hanbali school; Malik ibn Anas, founder of the Maliki school; and al-Shafi'i, founder of the Shafi'i school.

I once explained to a venerable shaykh the process we might call the “secularization of the spiritual,” in which something spiritual is reduced to an outward institution. He replied: “Something like that happened very early in Islam, when the teaching of our Imams was set aside in favour of the four founders of the legal schools. In that way, Shiite spiritual knowledge ('irfan-e shi'i) was pushed aside.” It is therefore a serious misunderstanding of Shiism to treat it, as some have tried to do in our own time, as simply a “fifth” legal school alongside the other four.

Haydar Amoli's Shiite answer is forceful from the outset. First, he says, these four scholars themselves firmly rejected the claim made by some of their contemporaries that they were the Prophet's heirs in matters of the sharia.
Second, they could not have claimed that rank in any case, because they did not possess ismat, freedom from error and sin—the special quality of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”

Third, their knowledge was the knowledge of religious law, the outward teachings ('ilm al-zahir). It was not knowledge received as a spiritual inheritance ('ilm irthi). It was knowledge gained by human effort and learning from outside ('ilm iktisabi).

The centre of the argument is this: prophetic inheritance cannot concern outward religious teaching simply as outward teaching. It concerns the inner meaning (batin) of that teaching. This is because the inheritance is walayat, and walayat is, by definition, the inner dimension of prophecy. Such knowledge cannot be gathered from outside or built up through a chain of logical arguments. Outward religious knowledge can be acquired through human effort and study. For that very reason, Haydar Amoli says, it is not knowledge inherited in the spiritual sense.
What is inherited must be knowledge of the inner reality. That is the knowledge the Imams possess as heirs of the Prophet, and that their followers—their “Shiites”—share with them.

Are the Prophet's famous sayings about scholars really meant to refer to people who study outward religious law, or indeed to any knowledge acquired from outside? Consider these sayings: “The ink of scholars is more precious than the blood of martyrs.” “The scholars of my community are the counterparts of the prophets of Israel.” Or, more simply: “Scholars are the heirs of the prophets.”

If we remember the account of knowledge given earlier by the Imams and their commentators, Haydar Amoli's answer is immediately clear. It would be absurd to say that every scholar in the world is an heir of the prophets. Looking closely at the Arabic wording, he argues that the saying should be understood as: “Those who are the heirs of the prophets are the ones called scholars.” These are the people through whom, after the end of prophecy that brings divine law, the hidden, inward prophecy (nobowwat batiniya) called walayat continues: the Imams and their followers.

There is an obvious objection. Surely even this inherited knowledge—the forms of divine wisdom we have been discussing—requires effort, deep spiritual discipline, and many sacrifices? Yes, Haydar Amoli replies, it certainly does.
But it would be wrong to say that discipline and study produce such knowledge. They prepare us for it. They make us able to receive it. They are the means of preparation, not the source.
Because “God acts not through causes, but within causes,” the gift God gives to each person does not depend on any particular cause. To make this clear, our author offers a comparison:
Imagine someone whose father has died, leaving him a treasure buried underground. To uncover it, the heir must work hard: he must dig and clear away the earth.

But his effort does not produce the treasure, as a logical argument produces its conclusion. The treasure is already there. All the heir has to do is open a way to it. So it is with everyone whose father—the True Adam (Adam haqiqi, the Verus Propheta, the heavenly Adam)—has left treasures of divine wisdom buried beneath the soil of their hearts.

We cannot explore here all the forms and workings of this knowledge received as a spiritual inheritance. Haydar Amoli devotes an entire chapter to it—the third chapter of Book Three of his great Jami' al-Asrar.

But we should at least consider his reading of Qur'an 5:70: “If they observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what God has sent down from above, people would enjoy the blessings above their heads and beneath their feet.” To observe the Torah, he explains, is to follow the outward requirements of the sacred Law. To observe the Gospel is to follow the Law in its hidden, inner meaning. To observe the Qur'an is to embrace the whole of it.

The verse therefore points to three connected ways of living the faith: shariat, the sacred Law and its rituals; tariqat, the mystical path; and haqiqat, the realization of spiritual truth. These correspond, respectively, to the three greatest prophetic figures: Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad. Through them, human beings become able to contemplate both the invisible realities of the spiritual world (haqa'iq malakutiya) and the visible realities of the world we perceive with our senses (haqa'iq molkiya).

We would also need to examine the long discussions in which our authors distinguish the different kinds of wahy, a message conveyed by an angel, from ilham, inspiration. Haydar Amoli argues that the greatest thinkers in Islam ultimately had to arrive at a form of knowledge he calls gnosis: direct spiritual knowledge, or mystical divine wisdom. From this Shiite perspective, he sketches a critical history of philosophy and theology in Islam.

But the expression we have just met again—the “True Adam,” or heavenly Human Being—invites us to consider a third kind of sacred knowledge. It may hold the secret of the famous account of the Prophet's vision that has already occupied our attention. This third kind can accompany the first two, wahy and ilham. It is called kashf, or “unveiling”: a disclosure of the divine to the person who experiences it. Mystics commonly use the word, though they do not all define it in exactly the same way.

Here it means an unveiling that takes place in the heart. It is spiritual, but it also reveals a visible form or figure (kashf ma'nawi suri). It therefore involves what we have called the heart's “spiritual senses” (hawass ruhaniya), of which our bodily senses are only an outward extension into the physical world. For centuries, Muslim mystics and seekers of spiritual knowledge have reflected on the famous saying attributed to the Prophet: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.”

One aspect of this saying is especially important. It brings us back to the moment when the Prophet, as an arif—someone who knows through spiritual experience—reaches the very heart of his walayat: the “Gabriel of his own being.” Haydar Amoli observes that if Moses could see the divine Essence in the Burning Bush, a vision of God in the form of Light or in human form is surely just as conceivable.

Our mystics agree that what Muhammad saw in this manifestation of God was his own “form”—the form of his soul (surat nafsi-hi)—because it was “the most beautiful of forms, inwardly and outwardly.” Ibn Arabi explains the same point in another way: a divine manifestation is always seen in a form suited to the person who beholds it. But we still need to understand what this means in specifically Shiite terms.

We have already encountered the Intelligence belonging to the “eternal prophetic Reality.” The Prophet spoke of it when he said, “The first thing God created was my Intelligence,” or “my Spirit,” or “my Light.” We recognized in it the heavenly Human Being: the first Intelligence, the first prophet “in Heaven.” Muhammad, as a prophet on earth, is the outward manifestation of this heavenly Being. What he saw in his vision, then, really was his own eternal Essence: the True Adam, the eternal Human Being, the first manifestation of God.

Yet to see oneself—to see one's own soul—implies that there is a self deeper within us than the self we ordinarily know: the soul of that very self. We know that the eternal prophetic Reality has two inseparable sides: the original reality of prophecy and the original reality of the Imamate. Its soul, spirit, and heart are its inner meaning, its walayat. And in the final age of prophecy, this inner reality appears on earth in the person of the Imam.

The Prophet and the Imam are, respectively, the Intelligence and the Soul—or the divine Word and the Spirit—of the original Muhammadan Reality. This is why the Prophet so often calls the First Imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib, “my own soul,” “my very self.” If the Prophet saw “his soul,” or “his self,” in a vision, he did so as an arif: as someone whose innermost being was walayat, the source of his prophetic mission. This vision did not belong to the outward mission he had been sent to carry out before the world.

That same saying about the Prophet's vision led spiritual thinkers to probe the meaning of the Imam as deeply as they could. At this depth, several sayings begin to echo one another: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord”; “Whoever has contemplated his own soul—his own self—has contemplated his Lord, that is, his Imam”; and finally, “Whoever dies without knowing his Imam dies the death of those who remain unaware.” Such a person dies without knowing “his soul,” without knowing “himself.” As we shall see again in Chapter Seven, certain sayings of the Imams illuminate these maxims. They help us understand how, and why, the Imam stands at the center of Shiite spiritual life: the search for self-realization understood through walayat.

The holy Imams are both the keepers of the Treasure and the Treasure itself: both the interpreters of the meaning and that meaning in its fullness. All the divine knowledge inherited from the prophets—knowledge that is, in this sense, direct spiritual knowledge—brings us back to the experience in which the person being guided discovers the Guide and recognizes himself in that Guide. This idea of a spiritual inheritance from the prophets also governs the succession of two great ages: the “cycle of prophecy” followed by the “cycle of walayat.” It places the spiritual seeker in an interval between the age of the “Seal of Prophecy” and the future appearing of the “Seal of Muhammadan walayat.” The two cycles are essential to Shiite understandings of prophecy and the Imams.
5. The Cycle of Prophecy and the Cycle of Walayat

The two cycles correspond to one another. Each is the other's mirror image. Together they suggest an enduring pattern running through sacred history. This pattern belongs to the history of spiritual meaning, not to history understood simply as a study of recorded events. Walayat is the hidden mystery of the Imamate: the inner truth into which the Imams initiate their followers. It is both what spiritual initiation reveals and the act of initiation itself.

When a believer inwardly professes the threefold testimony of faith, that person enters the special relationship of love and closeness to God enjoyed by God's Friends. The cycle of walayat—the age of God's Friends following the age of God's Messengers, or prophets—can therefore also be called the cycle of spiritual initiation.

The two cycles are held together by the figures each calls its “Seal.” The Seal of Prophecy (Khatim al-nobowwat), also called the Seal of the Prophets (Khatim al-Anbiya), is Muhammad. He closes the cycle in which prophets bring sacred laws. That cycle began with Adam and continued through successive ages, each named for its lawgiving prophet: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad.
But we also know that, from prophet to prophet, the hidden dimension of the eternal prophetic Reality was secretly present, accompanying each one.

Finally, during Muhammad's mission, it became openly manifest in the person of the Imam. The end of the cycle of prophecy thus marks the beginning of walayat in its own right. This new age does not prepare for another prophet bringing a new Law. It prepares for the coming of the One who will reveal the hidden meaning of all earlier revelations and thereby remove every restriction imposed by their merely outward forms.

Walayat endures; the mission of prophets who bring sacred laws is temporary. This distinction also lies behind the idea of universal or absolute walayat (motlaqa): a spiritual reality independent of the features of any one prophetic age, because it is present in all of them. The Seal of this absolute walayat is the First Imam, since the Muhammadan Imamate embodies the inner meaning of every earlier prophetic revelation. Walayat then takes the particular form of Muhammadan walayat (khassa). Its Seal is the one who completes the full company of the Twelve Imams: the Twelfth Imam, now the “Hidden Imam.” In this sense, the Imamate as a whole is the Seal of walayat.

This is a grand and coherent vision. Shiite writers, especially Haydar Amoli, could not understand how Ibn Arabi, the great mystical thinker, had broken its pattern by making Jesus the Seal of absolute walayat. In their view, Jesus, as the last prophet before Muhammad, is the Seal of Adamic walayat—the form of walayat associated with the successive lawgiving prophets from Adam onward.
